A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
anurans can learn to respond to novel predators, and that this can be mediated by cues from the predator’s diet.
tadpoles of five of the studied anurans responded behaviourally to chemical stimuli from an exotic invasive crayfish, and that these responses were mediated by cues from the predator diet.

the behavioural response to chemical cues from a novel predator is not universal across species, and that the presence of cues released during predation events is critical to elicit behavioural responses.
The main takeaway from our work is that
prey can respond to novel predators, even in the absence of co-evolutionary interactions, if chemical cues from consumed prey are present.
chemical cues from the predator’s diet are a key component in shaping the behavioural responses of prey to novel predators.
the presence of a novel predator in the environment may not be enough to elicit behavioural responses in prey.
